children.text: The passport - at first glance a simple document we need for travel, has evolved over centuries. It reflects history, culture, and technological progress. The passport's evolution tells the story of human movement, identity protection, and the control of state borders.
Ancient World

The roots of the passport go back to the ancient world. In ancient Egypt and Babylon, special documents were used to identify people. In ancient Egypt, during the early period of Islamization, a strict passport system was in effect, since no resident of a district could leave their place of residence without the authorities' permission; such a document was called a "sijill" and was made from papyrus.
These documents contained

: a physical description of the person, their social status, and family ties. All such documents that existed at the time were used to identify individuals and grant travel permission. Their purpose, alongside movement, was also to guarantee security.
From the Middle Ages onward, the passport became an essential document for permission to travel, allowing its holder to leave a city or country and move around.

For the first time, in the 14th century in England, King Henry V issued a document confirming a person's origin - which land they lived in, their ethnicity, and a visual description of the holder. In 1540, responsibility for issuing travel documents in England was given to the Privy Council. It was during this period that the term "passport" began to be used.

In the Islamic world, a document similar to the passport was available only to merchants and scholars, who received it to travel safely. As we can see, this document served as a source of trust even more than an official travel permit. At the same time, in medieval Europe, such documents were issued by local authorities and indicated the regions in which the holder was permitted to travel. It's also worth noting that until the 20th century, passports contained only text fields listing the holder's physical characteristics.
The Period Following the First World War

After the First World War, border control tightened, and the need for passport standardization arose, in order to prevent foreign spies from infiltrating and to prevent the outflow of skilled labor from countries.
In 1920, at the League of Nations conference, a standardized passport format was established for the first time, which proved decisive for the international use of passports.
The Second World War and the Cold War Period

During the Second World War and the Cold War period, the passport became a political tool. It was used both as an instrument of migration control and as a symbol of national status and trustworthiness.
During this same period, special passports for refugees emerged, for example the Nansen passport, which gave refugees the right to travel.
The Modern Passport

The development of biometrics and technology has refined the passport even further. Since 2010, states have used machine-readable passports, which contain the traveler's biometric and other data, such as a digital facial image and images of fingerprints and the colored ring of the eye.

The passport is not just a document, but a cultural artifact that reflects a country's identity. Today, some countries use national symbols and cultural features in their passport designs. For example, Norway's passport depicts the northern lights, while Australia's passport shows Aboriginal symbols.
The Future of the Passport

The introduction of digital passports and plans for their use is a current topic in various countries around the world. The EU is actively working on introducing digital travel passports, which will allow citizens to store all necessary information in digital format and use it while traveling.

The first country to begin working on digital passports is Finland. In August 2024, Finland launched a pilot program for digital passports, aimed at replacing physical passports with a digital alternative.

This initiative allows Finnish citizens to cross borders using digital passports built into their smartphones. Travelers participating in the pilot system can send their data to border authorities in advance, which speeds up the control process and reduces queues. The European Commission is funding this project, and if successful, plans are in place to introduce digital passports in other EU countries as well. Currently, the program is in the testing phase and its results are being evaluated. If the system works smoothly, its rollout across all EU countries is planned.
Conclusion

The passport's history begins as a simple permit that ensured the right to travel. Over the centuries, it has become an expression of international identity, security, and national identity. The passport's evolution shows us how the world has changed. And now, as biometrics and digital technology continue to develop rapidly, it's also interesting to consider what the future of the passport will look like. Perhaps one day the passport will become fully digital.
